teach.heading: The same chart behaves differently depending on what time it is.
teach.body: Futures trade nearly around the clock, but not every hour behaves the same way. The Asia session tends to be quieter and range-bound. The London session often brings the first real expansion of the day. The New York session — especially the Regular Trading Hours (RTH) open — usually brings the highest volume and the sharpest moves, since it overlaps with US stock market hours and news releases. The overnight session (after New York closes, before Asia picks up) is typically thinner and choppier, with less reliable structure. None of this means one session is "better" — it means the same setup can look completely different depending on which session it's forming in, and a trader who ignores the clock is trading blind to context she could easily have.
teach.dayliNote: "I'm not telling you to only trade one session. I'm telling you to know which session you're looking at, because a level in London and a level at the New York open don't carry the same weight." — Dayli Scott

experience.intro: Walk the same level through two different sessions.

steps.prompt: A setup forms during the quiet overnight session with low volume. Should you weight it the same as an identical setup at the New York open?

options.label: No — session context changes how much weight the read deserves
options.feedback: Right — the same-looking setup isn't equally meaningful in every session.

options.label: Yes — a setup is a setup regardless of time
options.feedback: Ignoring session context throws away real information about how much participation backed that move.

steps.prompt: The exact same level gets tested overnight, then retested at the New York open with much higher volume. Which test carries more information?

options.label: The New York open retest — more participation, more real signal
options.feedback: Right — more real participants means the reaction reflects more genuine agreement/disagreement.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: Volume differences between sessions are real information, not noise to ignore.

steps.prompt: A trader ignores session entirely and trades every setup identically regardless of the clock. What is she missing?

options.label: Context about how much real participation is behind any given move
options.feedback: Exactly — the clock is free context she's throwing away.

options.label: Nothing — session doesn't actually matter
options.feedback: Session behavior differences are real and worth reading, not irrelevant.

reinforce.question: A trader sees a clean-looking break of structure during the thin overnight session, then the exact same level gets retested with much higher volume at the New York open. What does session context tell her about which read to trust more?
options: The New York retest carries more weight — higher volume and participation make the reaction more meaningful
They're identical — session doesn't change how a break should be read
The overnight break is more reliable because it happened first

reinforce.question: Explain why a break of structure during the thin overnight session might deserve less confidence than the same-looking break during the New York open.
reinforce.modelAnswer: The overnight session typically has fewer participants and lower volume, so a break there can happen without much real conviction behind it. The New York open brings far more volume and participation, so a break at that time reflects a much larger, more genuine disagreement between buyers and sellers getting resolved — it's simply backed by more real information.
